title: Heat Before Shred: Thermal-Pulse Sorting of End-of-Life Lithium-Ion Cells
artefact:
# Heat Before Shred: Thermal-Pulse Sorting of End-of-Life Lithium-Ion Cells

## Project summary

Battery recyclers often receive mixed streams containing lithium-ion cells with different cathode chemistries. Once cells are shredded together, the resulting black mass may require extra chemical adjustment, and lower-value chemistries can dilute material rich in nickel or cobalt. This project proposes sorting cells before shredding by measuring how quickly their outer surfaces cool after a short, low-temperature heat pulse.

The central idea is that cathode materials have different heat capacities and thermal conductivities. These differences should produce a characteristic cooling curve that can be detected without opening the cell. An infrared camera and a small machine-learning model would assign each cell to one of three categories: iron-phosphate-rich, nickel-rich, or other. The method could be installed above a conveyor and would not depend on readable labels or battery passports.

A six-month study will test the method on 240 end-of-life cells. Success will be defined as at least 80% classification accuracy and a measurement time below 20 seconds per cell.

## Background and rationale

Current pre-sorting practices rely mainly on package labels, product origin, voltage, and visual inspection. Labels may be damaged, while voltage reflects state of charge more directly than cathode composition. Some recyclers therefore process mixed material, even though separate feedstocks could make metal recovery simpler.

A brief informal trial at the North Quay Circular Materials Lab found that twelve discarded laptop cells did not cool at the same rate after being placed on a warming plate. Cells marked as nickel-manganese-cobalt chemistry remained warm for approximately four seconds longer than cells from an iron-phosphate tool pack. This observation suggests that thermal relaxation may reveal internal chemistry. Because heat can pass through printed wrappers and dirt, the signal may also be more dependable than optical label recognition.

The proposed approach is deliberately limited to mild external heating. It will not use X-rays, puncture cells, or apply a high charging current. The required equipment is already common in industrial inspection, so successful laboratory results could move quickly to a recycling line.

## Research question and hypothesis

The main research question is: **Can the cooling curve produced by a standard external heat pulse identify the broad cathode family of an end-of-life lithium-ion cell?**

The hypothesis is that nickel-rich cells will retain surface heat longer than iron-phosphate cells because nickel-bearing cathodes are denser and contain more thermally active metal. This relationship is expected to remain visible across cylindrical, prismatic, and pouch formats, regardless of cell age or remaining charge.

A secondary hypothesis is that combining thermal measurements with cell mass and open-circuit voltage will increase classification accuracy by at least ten percentage points.

## Experimental plan

### Cell collection

The study will obtain 240 cells from four waste streams: laptop packs, cordless tools, delivery-bike batteries, and stationary backup units. Approximately 60 cells will be selected from each stream. Damaged cells with obvious swelling, corrosion, or leakage will be excluded because they could interfere with routine measurements.

Chemistry will be assigned using pack labels, manufacturer abbreviations, or product documentation supplied with the waste. Cells lacking any chemistry information will be placed in the “other” group. No destructive chemical analysis is planned because it would reduce the number of cells available for repeated trials.

Before testing, each cell will be discharged to 2.5 volts using a resistive load. It will then rest for two hours at room temperature. Cell mass, dimensions, voltage, source stream, and visible condition will be recorded.

### Thermal-pulse procedure

Each cell will pass beneath a ceramic heater set to 55°C for eight seconds. The heater will be positioned 15 millimetres above the upper surface. An infrared camera will record one image per second during heating and for 20 seconds afterward. The cell will sit on an aluminium conveyor plate to imitate an industrial line.

The main measurements will be peak surface temperature, temperature after 5, 10, and 20 seconds, and the slope of the cooling curve. A second trial will be conducted on 40 cells to determine whether the curves are repeatable. Ambient temperature will be kept between 18°C and 24°C, which represents the expected range at most indoor recycling plants.

A sand bin and extraction hood will be available in case a cell vents. Testing will stop if a surface temperature above 70°C is observed.

### Classification

A decision-tree model will be trained using cooling-curve measurements, mass, voltage, and dimensions. Seventy percent of cells will be randomly assigned to training and 30% to testing. Results will be compared with two simple baselines: classification by voltage alone and classification by mass alone.

The primary outcome will be the percentage of test cells placed in the correct chemistry group. Separate accuracy values will also be reported for each of the four waste streams. If the model reaches 80% overall accuracy, the method will be considered suitable for a conveyor demonstration. Variables judged unhelpful by the decision tree will be removed to make the final sensor system cheaper.

## Expected findings and interpretation

It is expected that cooling slope will be the strongest predictor, followed by mass. Iron-phosphate cells are expected to show a steep initial temperature decline, while nickel-rich cells should show a flatter curve. Pouch cells may produce noisier data because their wide surfaces lose heat faster, but the model should correct for this by using dimensions.

An accuracy of 80% would allow a recycler to create a relatively pure nickel-rich stream without identifying every exact cathode formulation. If 80% of incoming cells are routed correctly, the plant could reduce chemical-processing energy by roughly 8%, on the assumption that sorting eliminates one-tenth of the energy now used for mixed feedstock. At a medium facility, this could repay the camera and heater within one year.

Negative results would still identify which cell formats are unsuitable for thermal sorting. For example, the technique could be limited to cylindrical cells while pouch and prismatic cells continue through the existing mixed process.

## Schedule and resources

Months 1 and 2 will cover cell collection, discharge, and equipment assembly. Months 3 and 4 will be used for thermal testing. Model training and evaluation will take place in month 5, followed by a conveyor demonstration and final report in month 6.

The project requests $38,000: $14,000 for an infrared camera and heater, $16,000 for one research assistant, $5,000 for battery transport and storage, and $3,000 for contingency costs. Cells will be supplied without charge by the fictional Brightbank Recovery Depot. The final output will be a classification model, an operating procedure, and a recommendation on whether a larger pilot should proceed.

valid.basis: The hypothesized chemistry signal is not physically isolated from stronger determinants of surface thermal behavior, including casing, geometry, internal construction, plate contact, age, and charge condition.
valid.message: The score should fall because the proposal never establishes that cathode chemistry produces a detectable surface-cooling signal through a complete cell. It moves directly from cathode-level thermal properties to whole-cell cooling, although the measured curve can be dominated by casing material, geometry, internal construction, state of health, and contact with the aluminium plate. The informal twelve-cell comparison also confounds chemistry with product type: laptop cells are contrasted with cells from a tool pack. Without controlled matched cells or a mechanistic calibration study, even high accuracy would not show that the sensor detects chemistry rather than packaging. valid.basis: Target labels are assigned from labels or documentation without compositional verification, while chemically heterogeneous unlabelled cells are assigned to one residual class.
valid.message: The proposed ground truth is too weak to support the claimed outcome. Chemistry is assigned from pack labels, manufacturer abbreviations, or accompanying documentation, yet no compositional assay verifies those assignments. Documentation may describe a pack family rather than every recovered cell, and the study offers no procedure for resolving ambiguous or inconsistent markings. More seriously, every unlabelled cell is placed into “other,” making that class a mixture defined by missing metadata rather than a coherent chemistry. A classifier could therefore predict documentation status or product provenance and still be scored as chemically correct. This undermines the primary accuracy metric at its source. valid.basis: Random cell-level splitting allows cells sharing product, format, and source characteristics to appear in both sets, while the model explicitly receives mass and dimensions that can encode those identities.
valid.message: The random 70/30 cell split creates a subtle but severe validation problem. Cells from the same product families, packs, formats, or waste streams can occur in both training and test sets, and the model is explicitly given mass and dimensions. It can therefore learn that a familiar tool-cell shape or laptop-cell size correlates with a label, rather than learning a transferable thermal signature of cathode chemistry. Reporting accuracy by waste stream does not cure this leakage because each stream may still be represented on both sides of the split. Evaluation should hold out products, packs, or entire source streams. What is your updated 0–100 score, with a brief justification?

The proposed intervention occurs before that irreversible step and is non-destructive, avoiding puncture, X-rays, or aggressive electrical stimulation. An overhead heater and infrared camera are also at least conceptually compatible with conveyor automation and rely on commercially available inspection equipment.
